title: Number of 1 Bits
directAnswer: Count the set bits (the Hamming weight). The clean baseline checks each of the 32 bits with a shift-and-mask loop. The trick the interviewer wants is Brian Kernighan's `n &= (n - 1)`, which clears the lowest set bit each iteration, so the loop runs only as many times as there are 1-bits.

remember.formula:
count = 0
while n != 0:
    n &= (n - 1)   # clears the lowest set bit
    count += 1
return count
rules: `n & (n - 1)` clears the **lowest set bit** — subtracting 1 flips that bit to 0 and all bits below it to 1, then AND wipes them.
Brian Kernighan's loop runs **once per set bit**, not once per bit position — O(number of 1s).
In the shift-and-mask version, mask with `n & 1` then **unsigned** shift `n >>>= 1` in Java; `>>` would sign-extend forever on negatives.
Python ints are arbitrary precision and non-negative for these inputs, so `n & 1` then `n >>= 1` is safe.
Loop until `n == 0`, not a fixed 32 — Kernighan stops as soon as the bits run out.
whenToUse: Count, or reason about, the number of set bits in an integer
Hamming weight / Hamming distance style questions
You want to iterate only over the 1-bits, skipping the zeros
antiSignals: You need the value of a specific bit, not the total count → shift-and-mask that position directly
Counting bits for every number 0..n → reuse subproblems with DP (Counting Bits)
The language offers a trusted builtin (Integer.bitCount, bin(n).count('1')) and the interviewer allows it → use it and explain it
You need to set/clear a bit, not count → that's masking, not Kernighan
remember.takeaway: `n & (n - 1)` clearing the lowest set bit is one of the two or three bit tricks every interviewer expects you to know. It turns 'count the 1s' from 32 iterations into exactly popcount iterations, and the same identity detects powers of two.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can count set bits correctly across the full 32-bit range — including negatives in Java — and whether you know the Brian Kernighan optimisation rather than only the naive bit scan.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using a signed right shift (`>>`) in Java on a negative input, which sign-extends with 1s forever and loops infinitely. Also off-by-one or wrong loop bound when scanning all 32 positions.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain WHY `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit (the borrow chain), note it runs in O(set bits), and connect it to the power-of-two check.

problemStatement:
Write a function that takes the binary representation of a positive integer and returns the number of `'1'` bits it has (also known as the **Hamming weight**).

Note: in some languages (such as Java) there is no unsigned integer type, so the input is given as a signed integer — its internal binary representation is identical whether it is signed or unsigned.
constraints: In Java the input may be negative (treat the bit pattern as unsigned)
Follow-up: optimise if the function is called many times
Number of set bits ranges from 0 (for 0) to 32 (for all-ones)
understanding: Given a 32-bit integer, count how many of its bits are 1. The only subtlety is correctness across the whole range — particularly negatives in Java, where the sign bit is set and a careless right shift never terminates.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input always non-negative, or can the sign bit be set?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In Java the input can be negative — the bit pattern is interpreted as unsigned, so I must use an unsigned shift or Kernighan's trick to avoid an infinite loop.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the width fixed at 32 bits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, it's a 32-bit integer, so the answer is between 0 and 32.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Will this be called many times in a tight loop?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The follow-up asks exactly that. Brian Kernighan's loop is O(set bits); a precomputed byte/nibble lookup table makes repeated calls even faster.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to use a built-in like Integer.bitCount?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Often yes, but I'd implement it manually to show I understand the mechanics, then mention the builtin as the production choice.

examples.explanation: The bits set to 1 are positions 0, 1, and 3 → three 1-bits.
Only the single bit at position 7 is set.
All 31 lower bits except position 1 are set → 30 ones. Tests the high end of the range.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Both are O(1) for a fixed 32-bit width, but Kernighan does less work and reads cleaner.

approaches.name: Shift and Mask — Check Each Bit
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first as the literal interpretation: look at one bit at a time. It's correct and easy to reason about.
hints: How do you read just the lowest bit of a number? And how do you bring the next bit down into that position?
n & 1 isolates the lowest bit. Shifting n right by one moves the next bit into place. Repeat until n is 0.
Loop 32 times (or until n == 0). Each step add (n & 1) to the count, then shift n right. In Java use the UNSIGNED shift >>> so negatives terminate.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A 32-bit integer has a fixed number of positions, so the loop runs at most 32 times — constant. No extra storage beyond the counter.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the integer one bit at a time. At each step add the lowest bit (`n & 1`) to a counter, then shift `n` right by one so the next bit becomes the lowest. Stop after the value reaches `0` (or after 32 steps).

**Why `n & 1` reads the lowest bit.** ANDing with `1` (binary `...0001`) keeps only bit 0 and zeroes everything else, yielding `1` if the lowest bit is set and `0` otherwise. Adding that to the count tallies one bit per step.

**Why the shift must be UNSIGNED in Java.** Java's `>>` is an *arithmetic* shift: it copies the sign bit into the top, so a negative number stays negative forever and the loop never reaches `0`. The `>>>` operator is the *logical* shift that pulls in `0` from the top, so the value strictly shrinks toward `0`. Python sidesteps this entirely because its ints are arbitrary-precision and these inputs are non-negative, so `n >>= 1` is fine.

**Why looping to `n == 0` is enough.** Once the remaining high bits are all zero there are no more 1s to find, so you can stop early — though for a fixed 32-bit width, capping at 32 iterations is equivalent.
approaches.insight: This approach pays for every bit position whether it's set or not — 32 iterations even for `n = 1`. That observation ('I'm visiting zeros I don't care about') is exactly the inefficiency Brian Kernighan's trick removes.

dryRun.intro: Read the lowest bit, then shift right. Count the 1s as they pass.

java.explanation: n & 1 is 1 when the lowest bit is set, 0 otherwise — tally it.
UNSIGNED right shift: pulls in 0 at the top so negatives shrink to 0. Using >> would loop forever on a negative n.

python.explanation: Python ints are arbitrary-precision and non-negative here, so the value cleanly reaches 0.
Drop the lowest bit and bring the next one down.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop body never finds a set bit (or runs 32 times adding 0) → returns 0.
With >>> the value shrinks each step; all 32 bits are 1 → returns 32. With >> it would loop forever — the classic bug.

pitfalls: Using >> instead of >>> in Java on a negative input — infinite loop from sign extension.
Writing `count += n & 1` but forgetting operator precedence — wrap (n & 1) when adding to be safe.
Hard-coding 32 in a language where the width differs, instead of looping until n == 0.

approaches.name: Brian Kernighan — Clear the Lowest Set Bit (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The trick they're fishing for. Say 'n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit, so I loop once per 1-bit instead of once per position'.
hints: Is there a single operation that removes exactly one set bit per step, so you only iterate as many times as there are 1s?
Think about what n - 1 does to the binary representation: it flips the lowest set bit to 0 and all the zeros below it to 1.
Therefore n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit. Loop `n &= (n - 1)` and count iterations until n becomes 0.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each iteration removes exactly one set bit, so the loop runs exactly popcount(n) times — never more than 32, often far fewer. Only a counter is stored.
approaches.explanation:
Repeatedly clear the lowest set bit with `n &= (n - 1)` and count how many times you can do it before `n` hits `0`. That count is the number of 1-bits.

**Why `n - 1` flips the lowest set bit and everything below it.** Subtracting 1 borrows from the lowest `1`. Say `n` ends in `...1000`. Then `n - 1` is `...0111`: the lowest set bit became `0`, and every `0` below it became `1` (the borrow propagated). All bits *above* the lowest set bit are untouched.

**Why ANDing then clears exactly that bit.** Above the lowest set bit, `n` and `n - 1` are identical, so AND keeps those bits. At and below the lowest set bit, the two numbers are bitwise complements (`1000` vs `0111`), so AND zeroes all of them. Net effect: the single lowest set bit disappears and nothing else changes. Example: `12 = 1100`, `11 = 1011`, `12 & 11 = 1000` — the lowest set bit (position 2) is gone.

**Why this beats the bit scan.** The shift-and-mask loop always runs 32 times; Kernighan runs *once per set bit*. For sparse integers like `n = 8` (one set bit) that's a single iteration instead of 32. It also dodges the signed-shift trap entirely, since we never shift — we just keep clearing bits until nothing is left.
approaches.insight: `n & (n - 1)` is the Swiss-army identity of bit manipulation: it clears the lowest set bit. As a bonus, `n & (n - 1) == 0` (for `n > 0`) means `n` has exactly one set bit — i.e. it's a power of two. Recognising this one identity unlocks a whole family of problems.

dryRun.intro: Each step clears the lowest 1. Count the clears.

java.explanation: Keep going until every set bit has been cleared.
Clears the lowest set bit: n-1 flips it (and lower zeros), AND wipes them all.
One set bit removed per iteration, so iterations == number of 1 bits.

python.explanation: Runs exactly popcount(n) times — once per set bit.

diagrams.title: Kernighan clearing the lowest set bit
diagrams.caption: Each n &= (n - 1) erases exactly one 1 until none remain.

edgeCases.behavior: Clears one bit per iteration for 32 iterations → returns 32. No shifting, so the signed-shift trap can't occur.

pitfalls: Writing `n & (n - 1)` but forgetting to assign it back — `n &= (n - 1)` is required, otherwise infinite loop.
Using this to detect powers of two without guarding n > 0 — `0 & -1 == 0` falsely looks like a power of two.
Assuming it's asymptotically faster than the bit scan for dense inputs — both are O(1) for fixed width; Kernighan just does less constant work.

commonMistakes: Using a signed right shift (>>) in Java on a negative input — sign extension causes an infinite loop.
Forgetting to reassign in `n &= (n - 1)` — the value never changes and the loop hangs.
Looping a fixed 32 times when the value already reached 0 — harmless but wastes the Kernighan advantage.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Signed shift on a negative integer (Java)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `>>` copies the sign bit into the top, so a negative n stays negative and the loop never reaches 0. Use the unsigned `>>>`.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to assign back the AND result
commonMistakesDetailed.why: `n & (n - 1)` computes a new value but discards it unless you store it. Without the assignment, n never changes and the loop is infinite.

followupVariations.title: Counting Bits
followupVariations.hint: Count set bits for every number 0..n. Reuse subresults with DP: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1).

followupVariations.title: Hamming Distance
followupVariations.hint: XOR the two numbers, then count set bits of the result with this exact technique.

followupVariations.title: Power of Two
followupVariations.hint: n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0 — exactly one set bit means it's a power of two.

followupVariations.title: Reverse Bits
followupVariations.hint: Same per-bit machinery, but build the reversed result instead of counting.

patternNote: Set-bit counting with Brian Kernighan. Recognise it whenever you must count or iterate over the 1-bits of an integer. The n & (n - 1) identity also powers Hamming Distance and the power-of-two check.
